claims.claim: Personality is the long-standing traits and patterns that make a person consistently think, feel, and behave in specific ways; it is what makes each person a unique individual.

Personality traits are relatively stable characteristic patterns of thought, feeling, and behavior; trait psychology rests on the idea that people differ along basic trait dimensions that persist over time and across situations.

The Five-Factor Model (Big Five) describes personality on five broad factors — openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism (OCEAN) — each a spectrum; the factors have been found across ethnicities, cultures, and ages, and researchers including McCrae and Costa are associated with the model.

Freud's psychodynamic theory (attributed as theory, not fact) proposes that personality is shaped by unconscious forces and by conflicts among the id, ego, and superego, and that early childhood experiences shape adult personality; Freud was the first to systematically study and theorize the workings of the unconscious mind.
Maslow's humanistic contribution: the hierarchy of needs, with self-actualization — the achievement of one's fullest potential — at the top.

Rogers's humanistic contribution: self-concept (our thoughts and feelings about ourselves), congruence between the real self and the ideal self, and unconditional positive regard as a support for healthy development.

Bandura's social-cognitive view: personality develops through learning and cognition; reciprocal determinism means cognitive processes, behavior, and context all interact, each influencing the others; observational learning and self-efficacy also play a part.

Twin studies (the Minnesota study of twins reared apart, ~350 pairs, 1979-1999) found that identical twins raised in different homes have very similar personalities, suggesting the heritability of some traits; heritability is the proportion of difference among people attributed to genetics; traits arise from combinations of many genes plus environmental and epigenetic factors, not a single gene.

No single perspective fully explains personality; the field offers multiple perspectives (trait, psychodynamic, humanistic, social-cognitive, biological), each emphasizing different sources of personality, and trait psychology itself is debated (the person-situation debate).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Person-situation debate: how consistent are traits really?
positions: Trait theorists hold that traits are consistent and stable across situations and time (OpenStax 11.7; Noba personality-traits).
Critics of the trait concept argue people do not act consistently from one situation to the next and are strongly influenced by situational forces (Noba personality-traits).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both sides and reflects the modern both/and position: traits predict behavior on average across situations, while situations and learning (Bandura's reciprocal determinism) shape how traits are expressed. The social-cognitive section and the honest framing carry this nuance.

positions: Freud's theory of the unconscious, id/ego/superego, and psychosexual stages has been historically influential (OpenStax 11.2).

Freud's specific claims are controversial, partly untestable, and contested in modern psychology (OpenStax 11.2 framing of Freud as 'probably the most controversial and misunderstood psychological theorist').
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson attributes the psychodynamic view strictly as theory ('Freud's theory'), flags it as contested and hard to test, and does not present any Freudian mechanism as established fact.
